title: U.S. House · Iowa's 2nd District
area: Northeast Iowa, including Dubuque, Cedar Rapids-area suburbs, and Decorah

context.text: This is an open seat: incumbent Ashley Hinson (R) is running for U.S. Senate instead of re-election. Lindsay James (D), a member of the Iowa House of Representatives, defeated Kathryn Dolter and Clint Twedt-Ball in the June 2, 2026 Democratic primary. Joe Mitchell (R), a former Iowa state representative, defeated Charlie McClintock in the June 2, 2026 Republican primary. Rick Stewart (Libertarian) and Dave Bushaw (Independent) are also on the general-election ballot.

summary.text: James is a Democratic member of the Iowa House of Representatives from Dubuque, an ordained Presbyterian pastor, and a co-founder of the Loras College Peace Institute. She was first elected to the Iowa House in 2018, serves as House minority whip, and won the June 2, 2026 Democratic primary for this open seat.

background.text: Born in Portland, Oregon, James graduated from West Linn High School in 1999, earned a communications degree from Santa Clara University in 2003, and received a Master of Divinity from Fuller Theological Seminary in 2007.

She was a minister at Menlo Park Presbyterian Church (2007-2010), an interfaith chaplain at Endicott College (2012-2015), and an associate pastor at Westminster Presbyterian Church (2016-2017). She has been an adjunct instructor at the University of Dubuque since 2015.
In 2017 she co-founded the Loras College Peace Institute and served as its director.

She has served on the board of the Children of Abraham Interfaith Council, as chair of religious affairs for the NAACP Dubuque Chapter, and as chair of the Dubuque Community Development Advisory Commission.

James was first elected to the Iowa House in 2018 for District 99, winning an open seat with about 60% of the vote after Abby Finkenauer left it to run for Congress. She was re-elected in 2020, again in 2022 (after redistricting, in District 71), and in 2024.
Elected to the House Democratic leadership team as minority whip in 2022, she has served in that role since taking office in 2023.

Her Iowa House committee assignments in 2023-2024 included Government Oversight (ranking member) and Judiciary; in 2025-2026 they are Commerce, Environmental Protection, Judiciary, and Ways and Means.

James announced her campaign for Iowa's 2nd District on August 19, 2025, saying she would focus on health care and housing costs, and defeated Clint Twedt-Ball and Kathryn Dolter in the June 2, 2026 Democratic primary.
According to Wikipedia, she lives in Dubuque with her husband and their two children.

positions.summary: Campaign website calls for lowering the Medicare buy-in age to 55 and reversing Medicaid cuts.
positions.quote: I will work to lower the Medicare buy in age to 55

positions.summary: Campaign website calls for restoring Roe v. Wade as the law of the land.
positions.quote: Restore Roe v. Wade to be the law of the land and defend a woman’s right to make her own medical decision with her body.

positions.summary: Campaign website calls for closing loopholes, mandating background checks, red flag laws and an assault weapons ban.
positions.quote: We must close loopholes, mandate violent history checks, pass red flag laws, and ban assault weapons.

positions.summary: Campaign website says increased child tax credit investments should be financed by the ultra-wealthy and large corporations paying more.
positions.quote: We need to finance these investments by ensuring the ultra wealthy and large corporations pay their fair share.

positions.summary: Campaign website calls for cutting red tape so more homes can be built.
positions.quote: We must cut red tape and roll back tariffs on building materials so we can build millions of new homes.

record.text: Serves on the Iowa House Commerce, Environmental Protection, Judiciary, and Ways and Means committees (2025-2026).

candidates.name: Joe Mitchell
candidates.currentRole: Former member, Iowa House of Representatives (District 84, 2019-2023)

summary.text: Mitchell is a Republican businessman and former Iowa state representative from Clear Lake who, when first sworn in, was the youngest person elected to the Iowa legislature. After leaving the legislature he worked in the second Trump administration, most recently as a regional administrator at the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. According to his campaign website, he is running on fiscal responsibility, lower taxes, support for family farmers, and secure borders.

background.text: Mitchell was born in Wayland, Iowa, on April 23, 1997, and graduated from Waco High School in December 2014.
He earned a Bachelor of Science in business administration from Drake University in 2018.
He runs a real estate development business based in Clear Lake and founded Run Gen Z, a nonprofit that aims to elect young conservatives to public office.

Elected in 2018 to an open seat representing Iowa House District 84, he served from January 2019 to January 2023. He was sworn in at age 21, the youngest legislator in Iowa history, and was re-elected in 2020.
In the Iowa House he served as an assistant leader and on the Administration and Rules, Commerce, Judiciary, State Government, and Ways and Means committees.
After redistricting placed him in the same district as another Republican incumbent, he lost the June 7, 2022 Republican primary for District 87 to Jeff Shipley.
According to Wikipedia, he was a resident fellow at Harvard University in 2023 and joined President Trump's 2024 transition team.

In 2025 he served as chief of staff of the Federal Housing Finance Agency and then as the Trump-appointed HUD regional administrator for the Great Plains region, covering Iowa, Nebraska, Missouri, and Kansas.
He announced his campaign for Iowa's 2nd District on September 8, 2025, and defeated state Sen. Charlie McClintock in the June 2, 2026 Republican primary.

priorities.text: Fiscal responsibility, lower taxes, and smaller government.
Support family farmers and rural communities.
Public safety, secure borders, and national security.

positions.summary: Mitchell's campaign site says he will "protect the right to life."
Voted yes on HF 756 (removing the permit requirement to carry a handgun), which passed the Iowa House 60-37 on 2021-03-17.

stated.summary: Mitchell's campaign site says he will "defend the Second Amendment."

positions.summary: Voted yes on HF 2317 (replacing Iowa's graduated income tax with a 3.9% flat tax), which passed the Iowa House 61-37 on 2022-02-16.
Mitchell's campaign site calls the situation at the border a national security risk and emphasizes secure borders and lawful immigration.
Mitchell's campaign site says he will "support and fund the police while working for practical reform."
Mitchell's campaign site lists support for school choice among his education positions.

record.text: Served on the Iowa House Administration and Rules, Commerce, Judiciary, State Government, and Ways and Means committees (2021-2022).
Voted yes on HF 756 (removing the permit requirement to carry a handgun in Iowa), which passed the Iowa House 60-37 on 2021-03-17.
Voted yes on SF 413 (an elections bill shortening the absentee-voting window and tightening voter-list maintenance), which passed the Iowa House 57-37 on 2021-02-24.
Voted yes on HF 2317 (replacing Iowa's graduated income tax with a 3.9% flat tax), which passed the Iowa House 61-37 on 2022-02-16.

candidates.name: Rick Stewart
candidates.currentRole: Former CEO, Frontier Natural Products Co-Operative

summary.text: Stewart is the Libertarian nominee for this open seat, a businessman and former law enforcement officer who has repeatedly run for statewide and federal office in Iowa as a Libertarian, including for U.S. Senate (2020) and governor (2022).

background.text: Born in Postville, Iowa, Stewart was raised in Maquoketa and lives in Cedar Rapids, according to his 2020 Candidate Connection survey.

He graduated from Phillips Academy in 1969, earned an associate degree in agricultural mechanics from Kirkwood Community College, a bachelor's degree from Coe College (1991), and a master's degree from the University of Chicago (1993).
After traveling overland through Europe, the Middle East, and Asia for two years, he worked as a police officer in Maquoketa, according to his own survey responses.
He says he started the natural foods business Frontier Natural Products Co-Operative in 1976 and retired in 1999; Ballotpedia lists him as its CEO.

After retiring he says he traveled, including hiking the Appalachian Trail, and that he maintains an apartment in Guatemala where he works with an orphanage and school. Ballotpedia lists affiliations with EDELAC and Quetzaltrekkers in Xela, Guatemala.
Stewart ran as the Libertarian candidate for Iowa Secretary of Agriculture in 2018, U.S. Senate in 2020, and governor in 2022, losing each general election.

priorities.text: In a 2022 Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey completed during his campaign for governor, Stewart said he wants to end the federal Drug War and eliminate "crony capitalism," favoring limited government and a simpler tax system.
priorities.quote: I want to end the Drug War, America's greatest mistake and tragedy. Today, not when my grandchildren are grandparents. I want to eliminate crony capitalism, so we can enjoy all the benefits of the free market, with none of the corruption that comes from politicians with their hands in our pockets.

priorities.text: Says his top issue is eliminating nuclear weapons worldwide as quickly as possible (KCRG, Oct. 2026).
priorities.quote: So if the United States and Russia will just agree to eliminate our nuclear weapons, the rest of the world will go along with it because this is very important.

priorities.text: Says he wants to end the income tax and replace it with a land tax (Iowa State Fair soapbox, Aug. 2026).
priorities.quote: A land tax is the most fair tax of all.

positions.summary: In his 2022 Candidate Connection survey, Stewart said efforts to raise taxes on the wealthy don't work because they can hire lawyers and lobbyists to avoid the burden instead.
positions.quote: Trying to soak the rich never works, because they have the money to hire lawyers and lobbyists to soak us instead.

candidates.researchNotes: Stewart has not completed Ballotpedia's 2026 Candidate Connection survey and no campaign website was located. His 2026 statements come from news coverage of his Iowa State Fair soapbox speech (Aug. 15) and a KCRG interview (Oct. 14); the existing tax position and first priority are from his 2022 survey for governor and may not reflect his current platform.

statements.quote: When you put a tax on carbon, all of the people who are producing carbon, they start looking for waste to use less carbon because it costs more.

candidates.name: Dave Bushaw

summary.text: Bushaw is a farmer, folk and labor musician, and community organizer from West Union running as an independent. He says he is one of the youngest self-made, first-generation farmland owners in the U.S. and previously worked as a field organizer on Bernie Sanders' 2020 presidential campaign. He is running on universal health care, labor rights, and breaking from the two-party system.

background.text: Born and raised in West Union, Iowa; earned a high school diploma from North Fayette High School.
Describes himself as one of the youngest self-made, first-generation farmland owners in the U.S.; he owns a squash farm about 10 minutes from his childhood home, according to Iowa Public Radio.

Has been described as a longtime activist who began as an anti-war protester in the early 2010s; has worked as a community organizer for 14 years and traveled the country as a folk and labor musician playing for striking workers.
In 2019 and 2020 he was an organizer for Bernie Sanders' presidential campaign in Iowa, Nevada, and South Carolina.
Announced his independent campaign for Iowa's 2nd District in November 2025, saying that both parties "walked away from the people who built this country."

priorities.text: Says he is running to break from the two-party system, which he describes as "rigged against the Working Class," and is not accepting money from super PACs or AIPAC.
priorities.quote: The two party machine isn't broken. It's working exactly as intended -- rigged against the Working Class to the benefit of a small handful of billionaires and their friends in Congress.

priorities.text: Calls for national ballot initiatives so voters can decide directly on contested issues.
Says he will fight for a universal healthcare guarantee, arguing premiums, copayments, and deductibles function as "private taxes" on working people.

positions.summary: Calls for universal healthcare, saying the U.S. spends more than any other country while ranking poorly on healthcare outcomes.
positions.quote: We spend more for healthcare than any country on earth, but rank 14th in quality and dead last in healthcare outcomes. In America, we can provide our people healthcare as an American Guarantee and we can do it better than any other nation.

statements.quote: If they want to spend their own money waging conflicts in the Middle East and making enemies out of everybody, that’s on them.
statements.context: At a campaign stop in Tama, per the Tama-Toledo News Chronicle (Oct. 2026), in comments about Israel

statements.quote: I’m not anti-tariff, but I do believe that if we are going to have a robust tariff system, it needs to be coupled with infrastructure building incentives in the manufacturing industry.
We need strong borders if we’re going to continue the experiment of being the nation of America

candidates.researchNotes: No campaign website was located. Positions and priorities come from his 2026 Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey; the added statements are direct quotes from Iowa Public Radio (Nov. 2025) and the Tama-Toledo News Chronicle (Oct. 2026). Other positions in interviews (guns, labor, child care) were found only as reporters' summaries, so none were recorded.

researchNotes: Lindsay James's campaign website was under construction at the time of research, so no candidate-sourced priorities or issue positions could be documented for her beyond her state legislative committee record; only Ballotpedia background was available. Joe Mitchell's Ballotpedia page has no narrative biography, so his background draws on Wikipedia and news profiles. Biography gaps: no 2026 campaign website content was found for Lindsay James, Rick Stewart, or Dave Bushaw beyond Ballotpedia, and Mitchell's campaign site has no Meet Joe subpage content that could be fetched; Stewart's career details come from his own 2020 survey responses.
